distractor_explanations.Cause and effect: Reads 'reasons' as causal links; cause and effect explains why events happen, not a topic's supporting details.
distractor_explanations.Problem and solution: Equates supporting details with solutions; this structure centers on a problem and its fixes, not a topic's attributes.
distractor_explanations.Sequence: Assumes listing means ordering; sequence arranges events or steps in time, which the stem never mentions.

distractor_explanations.Simile: Looks for 'like' or 'as' and finds none; the passage never makes an explicit comparison between unlike things.
distractor_explanations.Onomatopoeia: Assumes the imagery is sound-based; no word imitates a sound, and the device at work is attributing human traits.
distractor_explanations.Hyperbole: Treats 'scar of consumption' as pure exaggeration; the phrasing grants the caterpillar deliberate, persistent intent instead.

distractor_explanations.Provide worksheets with multiple-choice: Relies on practice alone with no modeling; worksheets assess the skill but never demonstrate how to find a main idea.
distractor_explanations.Have students memorize the definition of: Treats knowing a definition as having the skill; students can recite the term yet still fail to identify one in text.
distractor_explanations.Assign students to underline every sente: Mistakes marking everything for analysis; underlining every sentence gives no criteria for judging which point matters most.

distractor_explanations.To summarize the entire chapter: Overstates a caption's scope; captions explain one visual, not the whole chapter's content.
distractor_explanations.To list the bibliography sources: Confuses text features; source lists belong in a bibliography or references section, not beneath a photograph.
distractor_explanations.To provide the table of contents: Confuses front-matter with captions; a table of contents maps chapters, while a caption sits with its image.

distractor_explanations.It is a dependent clause that modifies t: Calls the phrase a clause; it contains no subject and verb, so it cannot be a dependent clause modifying anything.
distractor_explanations.It is a prepositional phrase indicating: Overlooks that no preposition opens the phrase; 'a treasure trove of scrolls' renames the library as a noun phrase.
distractor_explanations.It is a compound predicate describing ac: Assumes a second action; the phrase names a thing rather than describing actions, so no predicate exists.

distractor_explanations.Appeal to emotion through vivid imagery: Labels the sentence emotional imagery; no vivid sensory detail appears, and the point is the intention-outcome gap.
distractor_explanations.Direct argument with supporting evidence: Sees persuasion where none exists; the sentence presents no claims or evidence, only an ironic reversal.
distractor_explanations.Simple chronological narration: Reads the sentence as a timeline; it reports no sequence of events but a contrast between intention and result.

distractor_explanations.Drill sight words repeatedly until autom: Targets decoding, which is already accurate; the student's gaps are in prosody and comprehension, not word recognition.
distractor_explanations.Assign more challenging independent read: Raises difficulty when the student cannot yet read accessible text expressively; harder passages deepen the gap.
distractor_explanations.Have the student read silently for longe: Extends the same unexpressive silent habits; without modeling and oral practice, fluency and recall do not improve.

distractor_explanations.Comma: Creates a comma splice; a comma alone cannot join two independent clauses without a coordinating conjunction.
distractor_explanations.Colon: Misapplies a colon; colons introduce lists or explanations rather than linking two related statements as equals.
distractor_explanations.Apostrophe: Confuses possession with clause joining; an apostrophe marks ownership or contraction, never separates clauses.

distractor_explanations.Entertain with stories of ancient forest: Mistakes informational content for amusement; the passage presents knowledge about controlled burning, not a story.
distractor_explanations.Persuade readers to move to rural areas: Reads a call to action into description; the passage shares information and does not urge readers to relocate.
distractor_explanations.Argue that all modern fire prevention po: Overstates the author's stance; presenting traditional practices is not the same as attacking every modern policy.

distractor_explanations.The project succeeded despite committee: Reads the sentence as fact; the inverted conditional signals the opposite, since the success never happened.
distractor_explanations.The committee acted on time and the proj: Reverses the implication; 'Had ... acted sooner' concedes that the action did not come early enough.
distractor_explanations.The committee was unsure about the proje: Finds doubt in the wrong place; the sentence implies regret about inaction, not uncertainty about scheduling.

distractor_explanations.Provide only simplified texts at their r: Lowers the text instead of scaffolding access; simplified texts block grade-level content and language growth.
distractor_explanations.Require students to read silently withou: Removes every support; silent reading alone leaves unknown vocabulary and structures unexplained.
distractor_explanations.Have students listen to the text without: Substitutes listening for reading; without seeing the text, students miss word-level exposure and decoding practice.

distractor_explanations.Opinions appear in textbooks; facts appe: Matches genre to factuality incorrectly; both facts and opinions can appear in textbooks or in editorials.
distractor_explanations.Facts are always longer than opinions: Ties the difference to length; fact versus opinion is about verifiability, not sentence size.
distractor_explanations.There is no meaningful difference betwee: Denies the distinction entirely; the core test is whether a statement can be verified or expresses a judgment.

distractor_explanations.Therefore: Confuses contrast with result; 'therefore' signals a conclusion that follows from a previous idea.
distractor_explanations.Additionally: Chooses an additive transition; 'additionally' stacks ideas rather than setting them against each other.
distractor_explanations.Consequently: Confuses contrast with consequence; 'consequently' shows a cause-and-effect link, not an opposing one.

distractor_explanations.\"Don't worry about it; poems are suppos: Dismisses the confusion instead of modeling strategy use; calling poems hard offers no move toward understanding.
distractor_explanations.\"The poem is difficult; just memorize t: Substitutes rote recall for thinking aloud; memorizing an idea bypasses the rereading and questioning that matter.
distractor_explanations.\"Ask your parents for help with homewor: Defers help outside the lesson; the teachable moment for modeling comprehension strategies is in the classroom.

distractor_explanations.un (root) + happy (affix) + ness (root): Swaps the labels; 'un' is the prefix and 'happy' is the root, with only '-ness' functioning as a suffix.

distractor_explanations.una (prefix) + happy (root) + ness (suff: Attaches the wrong letters to the prefix; 'una' is not a morpheme, while 'un-' alone is.

distractor_explanations.There going to the park after their done: Swaps both homophones; 'There' cannot act as the subject's contraction, and 'their done' misuses the possessive.
distractor_explanations.Theyre going to the park after there don: Drops the apostrophe in 'Theyre' and then misuses 'there' where the contraction 'they're' is required.
distractor_explanations.Their going to the park after theyre don: Uses the possessive 'Their' where the contraction is needed and omits the apostrophe in 'theyre'.

distractor_explanations.The experiment failed, the students trie: Keeps a comma splice; a comma alone still leaves two independent clauses improperly joined.
distractor_explanations.The experiment failed the students, trie: Mangles the meaning by making 'the students' a direct object; the comma placement separates nothing correctly.
distractor_explanations.The experiment, failed the students trie: Inserts a comma inside the first clause; a comma never belongs between a subject and its verb.

distractor_explanations.Circle 'was when' and write 'fix this' i: Gives a verdict without direction; circling errors shows what is wrong but not how to build a specific claim.
distractor_explanations.Rewrite the thesis for the student and h: Removes the student's ownership; copying a teacher-written thesis skips the thinking that revision requires.
distractor_explanations.Tell the student the thesis is acceptabl: Accepts a vague thesis; 'many things happened' names no specific claim and gives the essay nothing to prove.

distractor_explanations.Form refers to meaning; function refers: Reverses the two definitions; form describes a word's structure, while function describes its role, not its spelling.
distractor_explanations.Form applies only to verbs; function app: Limits both terms to single parts of speech; every word class has both a form and a role in a sentence.
distractor_explanations.Form and function are identical concepts: Collapses two distinct concepts; a word's structure can differ from its role, as when a noun functions adjectivally.

distractor_explanations.To copy vocabulary words into sentences: Confuses outlining with vocabulary work; outlines map essay ideas, not word lists.
distractor_explanations.To ensure perfect grammar in every sente: Expects grammar polishing at the planning stage; outlines arrange ideas before any sentences are drafted.
distractor_explanations.To replace the need for drafting: Treats the outline as the finished process; it is a planning tool that precedes, not replaces, drafting.

distractor_explanations.Have students only compliment each other: Limits feedback to praise; compliments feel safe but give the writer nothing specific to revise.
distractor_explanations.Allow students to review without any gui: Removes structure entirely; without criteria, students default to vague or purely personal reactions.
distractor_explanations.Tell students to find and circle all err: Turns review into proofreading; hunting surface errors ignores the content and organization feedback that matters.

distractor_explanations.'Although the data seemed accurate, seve: Keeps the passive construction; 'several discrepancies were found' still names no agent performing the review.
distractor_explanations.'Upon further review, several discrepanc: Reorders the clauses without adding a subject; 'several discrepancies' still cannot perform the reviewing.
distractor_explanations.The original sentence is already correct: Overlooks the faulty modifier; with no subject acting, 'upon further review' attaches to nothing in the sentence.

distractor_explanations.At least ten sentences: Confuses length with structure; paragraph quality depends on unity and development, not a sentence count.
distractor_explanations.Direct quotes from at least three source: Applies research-paper rules to every paragraph; quotes may support evidence but are not required in each one.
distractor_explanations.Complex vocabulary throughout: Equates fancy diction with quality; clear, appropriate word choice serves a paragraph better than complexity.

distractor_explanations.A comma splice contains three or more cl: Invents a clause-count rule; the distinction rests on punctuation, not on how many clauses appear.
distractor_explanations.There is no difference between them: Treats the terms as interchangeable; a comma splice is a specific run-on type that joins clauses with a comma.
distractor_explanations.A run-on is always longer than a comma s: Judges by length; a short sentence with two unpunctuated clauses is still a run-on.

distractor_explanations.Tell the student articles do not matter: Dismisses a real pattern; articles affect meaning, and these systematic errors deserve targeted attention.
distractor_explanations.Assign extra grammar worksheets on all E: Overloads the writer with every rule at once; focusing on one pattern makes practice manageable and transferable.
distractor_explanations.Correct every article error with red pen: Buries the message under corrections; marking every error before responding to ideas discourages the writer.

distractor_explanations.To summarize the entire paper in one sen: Confuses the introduction with an abstract; one sentence cannot hook readers, give background, and state a thesis.
distractor_explanations.To repeat the conclusion verbatim: Reverses the essay's order; conclusions echo introductions, but introductions are written to lead in.
distractor_explanations.To list all sources used in the paper: Confuses the introduction with a works-cited page; sources belong at the end in formal citations.

distractor_explanations.A new topic to consider is whether schoo: Opens a fresh topic at the end; conclusions synthesize the essay's argument rather than raise new questions.
distractor_explanations.In conclusion, I discussed pollution, re: Merely lists topics and stops; 'That is all' adds no synthesis, insight, or sense of closure.
distractor_explanations.Recycling is important because it helps: Restates a body-point claim without wrapping up; a strong conclusion looks back on the whole argument.

distractor_explanations.'The coach told the players running fast: Switches to gerunds without keeping the infinitive frame; 'told the players to ...' requires matching 'to' phrases.
distractor_explanations.'The coach told the players: run fast, d: Replaces the infinitive series with bare commands, changing the sentence's grammar instead of fixing parallelism.
distractor_explanations.The original sentence already has correc: Misses the broken parallelism; 'they should shoot' shifts from infinitive phrases to a full clause mid-series.

distractor_explanations.To replace the need for topic sentences: Overstates transitions' role; they connect ideas but cannot state a paragraph's controlling point.
distractor_explanations.To make sentences longer: Judges transitions by word count; they exist to show logic, not to pad length.
distractor_explanations.To add decorative language: Treats transitions as ornament; each one carries a precise logical relationship such as contrast or cause.

distractor_explanations.The title only: Reduces the main idea to the title; titles hint at the topic but rarely capture the author's full point.
distractor_explanations.The first sentence: Assumes the main idea is always stated first; it may appear anywhere or be implied across the passage.
distractor_explanations.A detailed supporting fact: Confuses a supporting detail with the central point; details back up the main idea rather than define it.

distractor_explanations.Making exaggerated claims: Undermines credibility; overstatement invites skepticism instead of trust.
distractor_explanations.Ignoring opposing viewpoints: Weakens persuasion; acknowledging and refuting counterarguments signals fairness and strengthens ethos.
distractor_explanations.Using emotional language exclusively: Relies only on pathos; emotion without evidence or expertise fails to establish the writer as trustworthy.

distractor_explanations.Have them read silently without help: Removes all scaffolds; silent independent reading leaves vocabulary and structure gaps unaddressed.
distractor_explanations.Skip reading instruction for English lea: Denies access to grade-level reading entirely; English learners need targeted support, not exclusion.
distractor_explanations.Use only simplified texts: Substitutes easier texts for scaffolding; simplification lowers rigor instead of supporting access to content.

distractor_explanations.To end a paragraph: Confuses the topic sentence with a concluding sentence; its role is to open the paragraph's line of thought.
distractor_explanations.To list sources: Confuses paragraph structure with documentation; sources belong in citations, not in the topic sentence.
distractor_explanations.To describe the setting: Applies narrative conventions to all paragraphs; a topic sentence states a point, not scenery.

distractor_explanations.Problem and solution: Confuses structure with a narrative arc; this pattern centers on an issue and its fixes, not on time order.
distractor_explanations.Compare and contrast: Mistakes similarity analysis for sequencing; this structure examines likeness and difference between subjects.
distractor_explanations.Cause and effect: Confuses causal explanation with time order; this structure explains why events happen, not when.

distractor_explanations.It makes the factories seem friendly: Misreads the tone; 'dominated' and the sentinel imagery suggest imposing watchfulness, not warmth.
distractor_explanations.It describes the color blue: Focuses on 'gray' as the point; the color word is detail, while the device is the comparison to watchful guards.
distractor_explanations.It compares factories to soldiers litera: Takes the comparison as literal description; the phrase is figurative, suggesting vigilance rather than soldiers.

distractor_explanations.Write everything in fewer words: Merely shortens the text; a summary selects the most important ideas rather than compressing every detail.
distractor_explanations.Copy the first sentence of each paragrap: Mistakes topic sentences for a summary; stitching first sentences misses ideas the author implies across paragraphs.
distractor_explanations.Make it as short as possible regardless: Makes brevity the only goal; an over-short summary can omit the essential ideas that define the passage.

distractor_explanations.Fiction is longer; nonfiction is shorter: Ties genre to length; both fiction and nonfiction come in every length from brief piece to book.
distractor_explanations.Fiction has pictures; nonfiction does no: Judges by illustration; both genres may include pictures, so artwork cannot define the category.
distractor_explanations.There is no difference: Erases the defining line; fiction is invented while nonfiction reports verifiable facts about the real world.

distractor_explanations.Memorize the dictionary definition witho: Skips the in-text skill; looking up definitions without using context fails to build independent word-solving.
distractor_explanations.Ask someone to tell them the answer: Defers to an outside source; asking others solves this word once but teaches no transferable strategy.
distractor_explanations.Skip the word and continue reading: Abandons the word entirely; skipping leaves a key science term unknown, creating a gap in comprehension.

distractor_explanations.Group work with no accountability: Drops the expectation to ground claims; without accountability, students offer opinions without citing the text.
distractor_explanations.Open discussion with no structure: Mistakes structurelessness for rigor; unstructured talk rarely requires students to quote specific passages.
distractor_explanations.Teacher-led lecture about the text: Puts the teacher between students and text; lecturing models citation but never requires students to produce it.

distractor_explanations.Repetition of sounds: Defines alliteration, not metaphor; sound repetition is a phonological device unrelated to comparison.
distractor_explanations.An exaggeration: Defines hyperbole; metaphor compares two unlike things rather than overstating a fact.
distractor_explanations.A question asked for effect: Defines a rhetorical question; metaphor states that one thing is another to draw an implicit comparison.

distractor_explanations.To confuse readers intentionally: Mistakes effect for purpose; irony asks readers to notice a contrast, not to lose the thread of the story.
distractor_explanations.To avoid stating themes directly: Confuses subtlety with irony; irony depends on a gap between expectation and outcome, not on withholding themes.
distractor_explanations.To make the story longer: Treats irony as padding; it is a meaning-making device, not a device for extending length.

distractor_explanations.Tell the student to slow down: Treats speed as the cause; the error is a phonics gap in the 'ough' pattern, not carelessness.
distractor_explanations.Have the student copy the word twenty ti: Relies on repetition without instruction; copying one word builds familiarity but teaches nothing about the pattern.
distractor_explanations.Remove the word from future readings: Avoids the teaching point; the word will recur, and dodging it leaves the underlying phonics gap unaddressed.

distractor_explanations.To repeat the introduction word for word: Confuses closure with copying; conclusions restate key points in fresh language, not verbatim repetition.
distractor_explanations.To introduce new information: Breaks closure; new content belongs in the body, where it can be developed and supported.
distractor_explanations.To list unrelated facts: Scatters unrelated details; a conclusion synthesizes the text's key points into one cohesive close.

distractor_explanations.Comma: Confuses two small marks; commas separate elements, while apostrophes signal ownership or contraction.
distractor_explanations.Period: Chooses an end-stop; periods end sentences and have no possessive function.
distractor_explanations.Semicolon: Confuses clause punctuation with possession; semicolons join related independent clauses.

distractor_explanations.A teacher's opinion that uniforms are ni: Offers opinion, not evidence; 'uniforms are nice' is a preference that cannot be verified or measured.
distractor_explanations.A photo of students in uniforms: Shows compliance, not impact; a photo proves students wear uniforms, not that distractions decreased.
distractor_explanations.A statement that uniforms cost money: Raises an unrelated objection; cost concerns the budget and never addresses distraction in the claim.

distractor_explanations.Asking students to spell vocabulary word: Tests encoding, not comprehension; spelling measures neither inference nor understanding of a text.
distractor_explanations.Asking students to identify the author: Checks surface recognition; naming the author requires no reading between the lines.
distractor_explanations.Asking students to recall a fact stated: Tests literal memory; a directly stated fact requires retrieval, not inference beyond the text.

distractor_explanations.To list facts about the setting: Confuses dialogue with exposition; setting details belong in narration.
distractor_explanations.To replace narration entirely: Overstates dialogue's role; it works alongside narration, not in place of it.
distractor_explanations.To confuse the reader: Mistakes a device for a flaw; well-crafted dialogue clarifies character and moves the plot forward.

distractor_explanations.For example: Signals illustration, not causation; 'for example' introduces a supporting instance.
distractor_explanations.However: Signals contrast, not cause; 'however' sets one idea against another.
distractor_explanations.Similarly: Signals comparison; 'similarly' links like ideas without making any causal claim.

distractor_explanations.Equal length stanzas: Confuses enjambment with stanza form; line runs have no effect on stanza size or symmetry.
distractor_explanations.A rhyming pattern at line ends: Attributes rhyme to enjambment; rhyme concerns end sounds, while enjambment concerns syntax crossing line breaks.
distractor_explanations.Clear pauses at the end of every line: Describes the opposite effect; enjambed lines carry meaning past the line break instead of stopping at it.

distractor_explanations.A KWL chart: Chooses a before-and-after learning tool; KWL charts track prior knowledge and questions, not character traits.
distractor_explanations.A word search: Offers a puzzle with no analytic value; word searches build word recognition, not character comparison.
distractor_explanations.A timeline of events: Tracks plot rather than character; a timeline orders events without mapping traits or similarities.

distractor_explanations.The rhyme scheme: Confuses poetic structure with word meaning; rhyme scheme describes verse patterns.
distractor_explanations.The author's biography: Pulls in the writer's life; denotation concerns the word itself, not its origin or author.
distractor_explanations.The emotional association: Defines connotation; denotation is the neutral dictionary meaning, separate from feelings a word carries.

distractor_explanations.It determines the book's price: Confuses literary craft with commerce; point of view has nothing to do with cost.
distractor_explanations.It changes the genre: Overstates the effect; genre is set by content and form, while point of view shapes perspective within a genre.
distractor_explanations.It affects the font size: Confuses narrative perspective with page design; typography is a layout choice, not a storytelling one.

distractor_explanations.Assign longer texts immediately: Increases load without teaching skill; longer passages give more chances to lose the thread, not tools to track it.
distractor_explanations.Have them read faster: Mistakes pace for support; reading faster typically widens cohesion gaps instead of closing them.
distractor_explanations.Skip cohesive devices: Ignores the exact problem; without tracking transitions and referents, readers lose connections between sentences.

distractor_explanations.To replace the text entirely: Overstates the role; diagrams supplement prose, and key information usually appears in both.
distractor_explanations.To decorate the page: Dismisses function as ornament; diagrams carry information, such as labeled parts or processes.
distractor_explanations.To waste space: Treats a text feature as filler; publishers use diagrams to clarify content that words alone convey poorly.

distractor_explanations.To list all sources: Confuses the thesis with a bibliography; sources belong in citations or references.
distractor_explanations.To entertain the reader: Misassigns purpose; entertaining may flavor a thesis, but its job is to stake the essay's claim.
distractor_explanations.To describe the format: Confuses content with structure; a thesis states an argument, not the essay's layout.

distractor_explanations.'Add more transitions' written in red: Gives a verdict without teaching; the student must still determine where transitions belong and which logic they signal.
distractor_explanations.Ignore transitions and focus only on con: Splits craft from meaning; ignoring transitions leaves the essay's logical flow unaddressed.
distractor_explanations.Rewrite the essay for the student: Removes the student from the revision; a teacher-rewritten essay models nothing the student can transfer.

distractor_explanations.'We did the research and the results wer: Fixes the passive but keeps vague wording; 'were good' remains imprecise and wordy next to 'yielded positive results.'
distractor_explanations.The original is already correct: Misses both problems; the passive construction is wordy and 'good' is too vague for formal research writing.
distractor_explanations.'The research that we did produced good: Still buries the actor in a relative clause; 'that we did' adds words without removing the wordiness.

distractor_explanations.A fragment: Confuses completeness with complexity; a fragment lacks a subject or verb, while a compound sentence has two full clauses.
distractor_explanations.A sentence with one independent clause: Defines a simple sentence; one clause alone, however complete, is not compound.
distractor_explanations.A sentence with a dependent clause: Defines a complex sentence; a dependent clause cannot stand alone and does not make a sentence compound.

distractor_explanations.Show several examples and have students: Mistakes imitation for understanding; copying models shows the product but hides the reasoning that produces it.
distractor_explanations.Give students a fill-in-the-blank templa: Relies on a frame without thinking; fill-in-the-blanks produce sentences without teaching how to choose content.
distractor_explanations.Assign a topic sentence worksheet: Assigns practice before instruction; a worksheet drills or assesses but does not demonstrate the drafting process.

distractor_explanations.She likes to hike, swimming, and to bike: Alternates infinitives with a gerund; 'swimming' interrupts the 'to + verb' pattern.

distractor_explanations.A clause cannot stand alone: Overgeneralizes from dependent clauses; many clauses are independent and fully able to stand alone as sentences.
distractor_explanations.A phrase is longer than a clause: Judges by length; the distinction is grammatical, since a clause has a subject and verb regardless of word count.
distractor_explanations.They are the same thing: Collapses distinct units; a phrase lacks the subject-verb core that defines every clause.

distractor_explanations.Peace!: Reads as slangy and casual; exclamation-point closings suit friends, not a formal note to a teacher.

distractor_explanations.Later gator!: Uses playful slang; informal sign-offs undermine the respectful, professional tone a formal email requires.

distractor_explanations.Rewrite the opposing view for the studen: Does the intellectual work for the student; a teacher-written counterargument teaches nothing about addressing views.
distractor_explanations.Tell the student the essay is incomplete: Replaces teaching with penalty; refusing credit offers no path toward strengthening the argument.
distractor_explanations.Praise the writing and ignore the missin: Skips the teachable moment; without a counterargument, the persuasion stays one-sided and less credible.

distractor_explanations.To separate items in a list: Confuses the semicolon's roles; commas separate simple list items, while semicolons join related independent clauses.
distractor_explanations.To replace a period: Overstates interchangeability; a semicolon links two related clauses, while a period ends any sentence, related or not.
distractor_explanations.To begin a sentence: Misplaces the mark; semicolons sit between clauses within a sentence and never open one.

distractor_explanations.Quickly: Picks an adverb; the '-ly' ending modifies verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs, not nouns.
distractor_explanations.Run: Chooses a verb; 'run' names an action rather than describing a noun.
distractor_explanations.Happyful: Trusts a noun-plus-suffix guess; 'happyful' is not a standard word, while 'beautiful' directly describes nouns.

distractor_explanations.Students only compliment each other: Removes critique from review; praise-only feedback is pleasant but never tells writers what to improve.
distractor_explanations.Students read each other's papers silent: Mutes the exchange; silent reading may familiarize peers with drafts but produces no feedback at all.
distractor_explanations.Students swap papers and circle errors: Reduces review to proofreading; circling errors targets conventions while ignoring content and organization.

distractor_explanations.A noun that can be touched: Defines concrete nouns; abstract nouns name intangibles like 'freedom' or 'courage.'
distractor_explanations.A noun that is always capitalized: Confuses abstractness with proper nouns; capitalization marks names and titles, not ideas.
distractor_explanations.A noun that has no plural form: Overstates a pattern; many abstract nouns pluralize fine, as in 'opinions' or 'ideas.'

distractor_explanations.Exclamation point: Reserves the exclamation point for strong emotion; declaratives state information and end with periods.
distractor_explanations.Comma: Chooses a mid-sentence pause mark; commas separate elements and cannot end a sentence.
distractor_explanations.Question mark: Confuses sentence types; question marks end interrogatives, which ask rather than state.

distractor_explanations.Memorizing sentence types: Treats sentence variety as memorized facts; without rewriting practice, the patterns never transfer to students' actual sentence openings.
distractor_explanations.Writing only simple sentences: Confines students to one pattern, guaranteeing monotony; variety requires practicing multiple structures, not fewer.
distractor_explanations.Counting words in each sentence: Focuses on length rather than structure; varying openings depends on how sentences begin, not how many words they contain.

distractor_explanations.A type of verb: Confuses antecedent with a verb category; an antecedent is a noun, not an action word.
distractor_explanations.A word that comes after another: Assumes position defines the term; an antecedent is whatever noun a pronoun refers to, regardless of where it sits.
distractor_explanations.A punctuation mark: Confuses a grammatical term with a mechanical mark; antecedents are words, not symbols.

distractor_explanations.Praise it without any feedback: Withholds all guidance; praising without feedback leaves the student unable to adjust register for different audiences.
distractor_explanations.Correct every sentence to sound more cas: Treats the writer's formal register as an error to erase; feedback should build audience awareness, not strip linguistic identity.
distractor_explanations.Reject the paper for being too formal: Devalues the writer's linguistic background; formality is a feature to discuss, not grounds for rejection.

distractor_explanations.To start a new paragraph: Confuses a within-sentence insertion with a paragraph-level move; interrupters add comments inside a single sentence.
distractor_explanations.To replace the subject: Mistakes an interrupter for a substitution; interrupters supplement the sentence rather than stand in for any element.
distractor_explanations.To end a sentence: Confuses interruption with closure; interrupters appear mid-sentence, set off by commas, dashes, or parentheses.

distractor_explanations.i love mathematics: Fails to capitalize the pronoun 'I,' which is always capitalized in English.
distractor_explanations.I Love Mathematics: Capitalizes every word as if the phrase were a title; 'love' and 'mathematics' are not proper nouns in a normal sentence.
distractor_explanations.I love Mathematics: Capitalizes a school subject name; 'mathematics' is not a proper noun and stays lowercase.

distractor_explanations.The class enjoyed read, write, and paint: Uses bare base forms after 'enjoyed,' which takes gerunds; the series is parallel but grammatically wrong.
distractor_explanations.The class enjoyed to read, to write, and: Is parallel in form but uses infinitives, which do not follow 'enjoyed' idiomatically; 'enjoy' takes gerunds.
distractor_explanations.The class enjoyed reading, writing, and: Mixes gerunds with an infinitive, keeping the original faulty parallelism in the final item.

distractor_explanations.Tell them to check tenses: Offers a vague directive with no procedure; students need a concrete method for spotting and evaluating tense shifts.
distractor_explanations.Ignore tense consistency: Leaves unintended shifts unaddressed; inconsistent tenses confuse readers about when events occur.
distractor_explanations.Use spell check only: Relies on a tool that flags spelling, not tense; spell check cannot judge whether a shift is intentional.

distractor_explanations.A preposition: Mislabels the part of speech; prepositions show relationships between words, while interjections express emotion.
distractor_explanations.A type of noun: Assigns the wrong category; interjections like 'Wow!' stand apart from the sentence rather than naming anything.
distractor_explanations.A linking verb: Confuses an emotional exclamation with a verb connecting subject and complement; interjections fill no grammatical slot.

distractor_explanations.It is always grammatically correct: Assumes voice determines grammaticality; both active and passive constructions can be fully grammatical.
distractor_explanations.It uses fewer words always: Overstates a side benefit; active voice is preferred for clarity, not guaranteed brevity.
distractor_explanations.Passive voice is never acceptable: Turns a preference into an absolute ban; passive voice suits cases where the actor is unknown or unimportant.

distractor_explanations.Tell the student to write shorter: Gives a goal without a method; the student needs modeled practice in spotting and cutting redundancy.
distractor_explanations.Underline every word and make the studen: Makes deletion arbitrary; cutting half the words by rule can remove necessary content rather than true redundancy.
distractor_explanations.Ignore wordiness: Allows the habit to persist; wordiness weakens clarity and rarely improves on its own.

distractor_explanations.A type of paragraph: Guesses at a structural category; a colophon is not prose organization but a publication note.
distractor_explanations.A character in a novel: Confuses a publishing term with narrative content; colophons belong to the book's production, not its story.
distractor_explanations.A method of citation: Confuses the colophon with citation formats; it records production details such as printer, date, and place.

distractor_explanations.Happy and joyful: Picks a synonym pair; homophones must sound identical, not merely share a meaning.
distractor_explanations.Fast and quick: Treats synonyms as homophones; both words mean rapid, but they are pronounced differently.
distractor_explanations.Big and large: Mistakes meaning overlap for identical sound; homophones sound alike but differ in spelling and meaning.

distractor_explanations.ABAB: Alternates the rhymes instead of pairing them; cat/hat rhyme as a couplet, then dog/log form the second couplet.
distractor_explanations.AAAA: Marks all four lines as one rhyme; dog and log do not rhyme with cat and hat.
distractor_explanations.ABBA: Encloses the second rhyme inside the first; the poem pairs lines 1-2 and 3-4, not an envelope pattern.

distractor_explanations.They are the same: Collapses two distinct concepts; denotation is the literal definition while connotation adds emotional association.
distractor_explanations.Connotation is literal; denotation is em: Swaps the two terms; the dictionary meaning is denotation, and the emotional layer is connotation.
distractor_explanations.Neither has anything to do with meaning: Dismisses both as irrelevant; both terms describe layers of a word's meaning.

distractor_explanations.It confuses the reader: Mistakes structural complexity for confusion; the past-present contrast is purposeful, guiding readers toward change over time.
distractor_explanations.It has no literary purpose: Denies the author intent; juxtaposing memories with reality is a deliberate structural choice.
distractor_explanations.It makes the passage longer: Reduces structure to word count; the juxtaposition creates meaning, not merely length.

distractor_explanations.Assigning the same text daily: Confuses repetition with endurance building; stamina grows through sustained reading of varied texts.
distractor_explanations.Reading only short passages: Keeps reading sessions brief, so students never practice sustaining attention over longer texts.
distractor_explanations.Avoiding difficult texts: Shields students from productive struggle; stamina requires working through challenging material.

distractor_explanations.A chapter heading: Confuses a structural label with an epigraph's thematic function; epigraphs quote other texts, headings merely title.
distractor_explanations.A type of paragraph: Mislabels the term as prose structure; an epigraph is a borrowed quotation, not a paragraph form.
distractor_explanations.A character's thoughts: Confuses narration with front matter; an epigraph sits at the work's opening, outside the story.

distractor_explanations.To confuse readers: Assumes the effect is random puzzlement; the point is productive irony, where readers see what the narrator cannot.
distractor_explanations.It is required by the genre: Invents a genre rule; no genre mandates unreliable narration, which is an authorial choice.
distractor_explanations.Because they cannot write well: Mistakes a deliberate technique for a skill deficit; unreliable narration requires careful authorial control.

distractor_explanations.Read faster: Speeds up without building comprehension; summarizing depends on identifying key ideas, not pace.
distractor_explanations.More decoding practice: Targets a skill the student already has; the gap lies in distinguishing main ideas from minor details.
distractor_explanations.Skip summarizing: Removes the skill instead of teaching it; summarization is essential and can be scaffolded.

distractor_explanations.To introduce characters randomly: Mistakes deliberate hints for arbitrary placement; foreshadowing is planned, not random.
distractor_explanations.To summarize the plot: Confuses a forward-pointing hint with a recap; foreshadowing suggests the future rather than restating what happened.
distractor_explanations.To describe settings: Confuses foreshadowing with description; its function is anticipation, not scene painting.

Describes motion without imitating sound; onomatopoeia requires words that echo the noise itself.
States a physical attribute; no sound is reproduced in language.
Uses a figurative adjective for temperature; 'bitter' describes sensation, not a sound.

distractor_explanations.Creative writing: Targets composition rather than analysis; the needed skill is evaluating the account's bias and gaps.
distractor_explanations.Memorization: Reinforces the one-sided version instead of questioning it; retention is not the issue.
distractor_explanations.Speed reading: Increases pace without adding evaluation; faster reading of a biased source still accepts its framing.

distractor_explanations.Reading without attention: Undermines visualization, which depends on attending closely to descriptive language.
distractor_explanations.Reading quickly: Prioritizes pace over imagery; visualization requires pausing to form mental pictures.
distractor_explanations.Skipping descriptions: Discards the very passages that supply images; descriptions are the raw material for visualization.

distractor_explanations.A punctuation mark: Confuses a wordplay term with mechanical symbols; palindromes are words or phrases, not marks.
distractor_explanations.A type of poem: Overcategorizes; the term covers any word or phrase reading the same both ways, not just poems.
distractor_explanations.A character type: Confuses wordplay with narrative roles; palindromes concern spelling, not characterization.

distractor_explanations.It makes reading easier: Reverses the effect; non-linear structure demands more active reconstruction from readers, not less.
distractor_explanations.It has no effect: Denies the structural choice any function; fragmented timelines deliberately create suspense and engagement.
distractor_explanations.It is always confusing: Overgeneralizes from difficulty to confusion; skilled writers use non-linearity purposefully and readers can follow it.

distractor_explanations.Skip abstract texts: Avoids the challenge instead of scaffolding it; students still need to handle abstract ideas.
distractor_explanations.Define terms only: Provides vocabulary without understanding; definitions alone leave concepts disconnected from experience.
distractor_explanations.More abstract texts: Increases difficulty without support; more exposure to abstraction does not build access to it.

distractor_explanations.A character name: Confuses a literary device with an element of the cast; motifs are recurring images or ideas, not labels.
distractor_explanations.A plot twist: Mistakes a one-time event for a repeated pattern; motifs recur throughout the work.
distractor_explanations.A single symbol: Drops the recurrence requirement; a motif is a symbol whose repetition across the text builds significance.

distractor_explanations.A connecting word: Describes a conjunction instead; adverbs modify verbs and adjectives rather than joining elements.
distractor_explanations.A naming word: Defines a noun; adverbs describe actions and qualities instead of naming things.
distractor_explanations.An action word: Defines a verb; adverbs tell how, when, or to what extent about the action rather than being the action.

Contains an idiom, but 'kick the bucket' means to die, not to identify an issue precisely.
distractor_explanations.The carpenter struck a nail with a hamme: Reads the idiom's words literally; an actual hammering event is not the figurative expression.
